article.title: Why a Larger Sample Does Not Fix a Biased Experiment
article.why: Separate sampling uncertainty from systematic bias in experiment design.

paragraphs.en:
Large samples are powerful because they reduce random sampling error. If an experiment has only a few hundred customers, treatment and control results can move substantially because of chance. With hundreds of thousands of customers, estimates are usually more precise. But precision is not the same as correctness. A large sample cannot automatically repair a biased experiment.

Suppose a campaign sends treatment messages only to customers who opened the app recently, while the control group includes all eligible customers. With enough observations, the measured difference may become extremely precise, but it still compares different populations. The estimate can be precisely wrong.

Selection bias is one source of this problem. Another is inconsistent eligibility. If treatment customers are filtered using one set of rules and control customers using another, adding more customers simply reproduces the inconsistency at larger scale. Contamination can also matter: control customers may accidentally receive the treatment through another channel, reducing the contrast between groups.

Timing creates similar issues. Imagine treatment is assigned on Monday but control is extracted on Friday after some customers have already purchased. The groups no longer represent the same decision point. A million records will not correct this temporal mismatch.

This distinction can be understood through variance and bias. Increasing sample size usually reduces variance: repeated estimates become less noisy. Systematic design errors create bias: estimates are shifted away from the causal effect we want. More observations can make the confidence interval narrower around that biased value, giving a false sense of certainty.

Before increasing sample size, teams should therefore audit the experiment process. Were treatment and control drawn from the same eligible population? Was assignment random and performed at the same time? Were exclusions applied consistently? Could customers appear in both groups? Could control customers receive treatment elsewhere? Were outcomes measured over the same window?

Stratification and larger samples are useful after these foundations are sound. They can improve precision and ensure enough observations in important subgroups. But they are not substitutes for a valid assignment mechanism.

The practical lesson is simple: sample size solves a quantity-of-information problem, not a design-validity problem. When an experiment looks suspicious, asking for more data should not be the first response. First verify how customers entered each group and whether treatment was the only systematic difference between them. Then additional sample size can do what it is good at—making a valid estimate more precise.
paragraphs.zh:
大樣本能降低 random sampling error、提高 precision，但不能自動修正 biased experiment。若 treatment 只包含近期開 app 的顧客，而 control 包含全部 eligible customers，再多樣本也只是更精確地比較兩個不同 population。

Selection bias、eligibility 規則不一致、control contamination、不同抽取時間等都屬於 design problem。增加樣本主要降低 variance，卻不會消除 systematic bias，甚至可能讓 confidence interval 很窄，造成「非常確定但答案錯了」的錯覺。擴大樣本前應先 audit assignment、eligibility、exclusion、timing、cross-group contamination 與 outcome window。
paragraphs.ja:
大sampleはrandom errorを減らしてprecisionを上げますが、biased experimentを自動修正しません。treatmentだけ最近appを開いた顧客、controlは全eligible customerなら、件数を増やしても異なるpopulationを精密に比較するだけです。

selection bias、eligibility ruleの不一致、control contamination、抽出timingのずれはdesign problemです。sample size増加は主にvarianceを下げますがsystematic biasは消しません。むしろbiased valueの周囲に狭いconfidence intervalができ、誤った確信を強めることがあります。まずassignment、eligibility、exclusion、timing、contamination、outcome windowをauditし、その後でsampleを増やすべきです。

vocabulary.usage: A larger sample does not remove bias.
Treatment should be the only systematic difference.
Sample size cannot replace design validity.

business.term: A large sample can make a biased estimate more precise, not more correct.

sources: Randomized experiment design; bias-variance distinction; contamination and eligibility controls.
